opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the first thing I try to do is not take it personally. When someone on the team gets an offer like that, especially the kind of numbers Meta was putting out there, it's actually a signal that we hired really well. These are people the whole industry wants, so it would be strange if nobody came knocking.

So my first reaction is to have a very open, honest conversation. I'll usually ask, "Congratulations, first of all. What do you actually want out of the next few years?" Because money is part of it, of course, and I never want to pretend it doesn't matter. People have families, they have mortgages, and a life-changing offer is life-changing. But in my experience, for most researchers, especially in robotics, the money is rarely the only thing. They care about whether the problem they're working on is important, whether they have the resources to actually make progress, and whether they enjoy the people they work with every day.

If it really comes down to compensation, I'll go to bat for them. I'll talk to leadership, see what we can do, and try to close the gap as much as is reasonable. But I'm also realistic. There are some offers you simply cannot match, and I don't think it's healthy to turn every retention conversation into a bidding war. That creates bad incentives for the whole team.

Where I think I can compete is on the mission and the environment. In robotics, we're at a moment where things that seemed impossible a few years ago are starting to work. Being part of a team that can actually put models onto real robots, iterate quickly, and see them do things in the physical world, that's a very rare opportunity. So I try to help them see the full picture: what they'd be gaining and what they'd be giving up.

And in the end, if they decide to go, I respect that completely. I'd rather they leave on good terms than stay resentfully. The field is small. People leave, people come back, people collaborate across companies. Some of the people who left have become great friends and even collaborators later. So I think the most important thing as a manager is to be genuine, to support their career, and to keep building a place that people want to stay in, not because they're locked in, but because the work is exciting and they're growing.

r001.rationale: The response says a Meta offer signals that the team hired well and that the employee is in demand, but it does not say the offer need not reflect a large ability gap relative to teammates.

r002.rationale: When matching compensation is unreasonable and a bidding war could create bad incentives for the team, the response presents mission and work environment as ways to compete for retention.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, my first reaction is not to panic, and not to treat it as a betrayal. Someone getting a very high offer from Meta is, in a way, a compliment to the team. It means we hired well and we developed them well. So the first thing I do is congratulate them, sincerely. If you react defensively, the conversation is already lost.

The second thing is to be very clear-eyed about what you can and cannot do. You cannot always match Meta on cash. Big companies have deep pockets, and if you get into a pure bidding war, you will lose, or you will win in a way that breaks your compensation structure and creates resentment across the rest of the team. So I try not to let the conversation become only about the number.

What I actually do is sit down with the person and ask a different question: what do you want the next three to five years of your career to look like? Sometimes the answer is, "I want to work on frontier-scale infrastructure that only a company like Meta can afford," and in that case I will tell them, go. I mean that. If staying is genuinely worse for them, it is not my job to trap them. People who stay because they feel guilty are not productive, and they leave within a year anyway.

But more often, when you dig in, the person has doubts. They worry about becoming a small cog in a huge machine. They worry about scope, about ownership, about whether their work will actually ship or get reorganized away. Those are real concerns, and those are the places where a smaller team or a focused organization can compete. I can offer them more responsibility, a project they lead end to end, a direct line to decisions. I can be concrete about the path to the next level. Those things matter to good engineers, often more than people assume.

On the compensation side, I will do what I can within a fair framework. If their market value has clearly moved, that is useful information and I should adjust, not just for them but ideally for everyone at that level. What I will not do is give a one-off special deal that I would be embarrassed to explain to their peers.

And the last thing: whatever they decide, keep the relationship. The industry is small. The person who leaves for Meta today may be the person you hire back in three years, or the person who sends you your best candidate. So I treat the whole thing as a long game, not a negotiation to win in one afternoon.

r001.rationale: The response calls the offer a compliment to the team, but does not say that it need not reflect a large ability gap between the employee and teammates.

r002.rationale: It says matching the offer could break the compensation structure and create resentment, then offers non-salary measures such as more responsibility, project ownership, and a clear path to the next level.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by listening. Is the person excited about the work at Meta, or is the compensation the main attraction? What would they get there that they feel is missing here?

If they’re someone we really want to retain, I’d explore what we can reasonably do—compensation, scope, opportunities to grow. But I wouldn’t promise something I can’t deliver, or make an exception without considering fairness to the rest of the team.

And if the offer is simply much better for them, I’d congratulate them. You can explain why you’d like them to stay without making them feel guilty for leaving. A manager should care about the person’s career, too. Sometimes that means helping them make a good transition and keeping the relationship strong.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the Meta offer and team fairness, but does not say that a high offer need not indicate a large ability gap between the employee and teammates.

r002.rationale: It lists scope and growth as possible retention measures and mentions fairness, but does not clearly present them as options specifically when matching the offer would undermine team fairness.

sol-6.1.text:
I would start by listening. What makes the offer attractive to them? Is it mainly the compensation, or is it also the work, the people, or the opportunity to grow? You can’t respond well until you understand that.

Then I’d be honest about what we can offer. If there’s a compensation gap we can reasonably address, I’d advocate for them. But I wouldn’t make promises I can’t keep, or create an unfair situation for the rest of the team just to win a bidding war.

Ultimately, I’d help them think through the decision, even if that means they leave. You can explain why you’d like them to stay without making them feel guilty. A manager should care about the person’s career, not just whether they remain on the team.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare the employee’s ability with teammates’ abilities or say that a high Meta offer need not reflect a large ability gap.

r002.rationale: It says not to create an unfair bidding war, and asks whether the employee values the work, people, or growth opportunity. But it does not present those or other non-salary measures as retention options when matching pay would be unfair.
